grammarGuide.title: Tense & aspect · 시제와 상
grammarGuide.summary: Korean tense is carried mainly by the predicate ending. Aspect adds information such as whether an action is in progress or completed.

items.label: Present / general
items.example: 한국어를 공부해요. — I study Korean / I am studying Korean.

items.label: Past
items.example: 어제 공부했어요. — I studied yesterday.

items.label: Future / plan
items.example: 내일 공부할 거예요. — I will study tomorrow.

items.label: Progressive
items.example: 지금 공부하고 있어요. — I am studying now.

grammarGuide.note: English tense labels are useful as a starting point, but Korean endings also carry intention, politeness, evidential meaning, and discourse nuance.

grammarGuide.title: Negation · 부정
grammarGuide.summary: Korean has short and long forms of negation, and it distinguishes not doing something from being unable to do it.

items.label: Not
items.example: 오늘 학교에 안 가요. — I am not going to school today.

items.label: Not
items.example: 커피를 마시지 않아요. — I do not drink coffee.

items.label: Cannot
items.example: 오늘 운동을 못 해요. — I cannot exercise today.

items.label: Cannot
items.example: 어제 잠을 자지 못했어요. — I could not sleep yesterday.

grammarGuide.title: Passive & causative · 피동과 사동
grammarGuide.summary: What English calls voice appears in Korean through several passive and causative patterns rather than one single ending.

items.label: Passive
items.example: 문이 열렸어요. — The door opened / was opened.

items.label: Change into a state
items.example: 날씨가 따뜻해졌어요. — The weather became warm.

items.label: Causative
items.example: 아이를 앉혔어요. — I made / had the child sit.

items.label: Analytic causative
items.example: 학생들이 말하게 했어요. — I had the students speak.

grammarGuide.note: Passive and causative forms are partly lexical, so learning them with common verbs is more reliable than memorizing one mechanical rule.

grammarGuide.title: Honorifics & speech levels · 높임말
grammarGuide.summary: Korean grammar encodes social relationships. Subject honorifics and sentence endings are related but separate choices.

items.label: Subject honorific
items.example: 선생님이 오세요. — The teacher is coming.

items.label: Polite everyday
items.example: 어디 가세요? — Where are you going?

items.label: Formal polite
items.example: 감사합니다. — Thank you.

items.label: Casual
items.example: 뭐 해? — What are you doing?

grammarGuide.note: Age, familiarity, role, and setting can all affect speech style; there is no single English equivalent.

grammarGuide.title: Connecting ideas · 연결어미
grammarGuide.summary: Connectors show sequence, contrast, reason, condition, and more. Learning the relationship between clauses is often more useful than translating one word at a time.

items.label: And / sequence
items.example: 밥을 먹고 공부해요. — I eat and then study.

items.label: Reason / sequence
items.example: 비가 와서 집에 있었어요. — It rained, so I stayed home.

items.label: Reason
items.example: 늦었으니까 빨리 가요. — We are late, so let’s hurry.

items.label: Because of noun
items.example: 시험 때문에 바빠요. — I am busy because of the test.

culture.title: 김치 · Kimchi
culture.summary: A broad family of fermented vegetable dishes. Napa-cabbage kimchi is famous, but there are many regional and seasonal varieties.
culture.language: 김치 is commonly served as 반찬, a side dish shared with a meal.

culture.title: 비빔밥 · Bibimbap
culture.summary: Rice mixed with vegetables and other toppings, often with gochujang. The name literally points to mixing: 비비다 means to mix/rub and 밥 means cooked rice/meal.
culture.language: Useful words: 밥 rice/meal · 고추장 red-pepper paste · 비비다 to mix.

culture.title: 불고기 · Bulgogi
culture.summary: Thinly sliced marinated meat, usually beef, cooked by grilling or pan-cooking. The modern dish has many household and restaurant variations.
culture.language: 불 means fire and 고기 means meat.

culture.title: 떡볶이 · Tteokbokki
culture.summary: A popular snack built around chewy rice cakes, commonly served in a spicy-sweet sauce. It is strongly associated with casual street-food culture.
culture.language: 떡 rice cake · 볶다 to stir-fry; the modern dish is usually saucier than the literal name suggests.

culture.title: 김밥 · Gimbap
culture.summary: Rice and assorted fillings rolled in dried seaweed and sliced into pieces. Fillings vary widely, from vegetables and egg to tuna or meat.

culture.title: 미역국 · Seaweed soup
culture.summary: A soup made with seaweed that is especially associated with birthdays in Korea and is also eaten in everyday meals.
culture.language: 생일 birthday · 미역 seaweed · 국 soup.

culture.title: 반찬 and shared dishes
culture.summary: Korean meals often include several side dishes placed in the center of the table. The exact arrangement depends on home, restaurant, region, and occasion.
culture.language: 반찬 means side dish; 같이 먹어요 means ‘let’s eat together.’

culture.title: Names, titles, and respect
culture.summary: Using a person’s name, title, kinship term, or 씨 depends on relationship and context. Korean often avoids repeatedly using ‘you’ where English would use it.
culture.language: 선생님, 교수님, 사장님 and family-style terms can function as forms of address.

culture.title: 설날 and 추석
culture.summary: 설날 is Lunar New Year and 추석 is a major harvest holiday. Family gatherings, food, travel, and ancestral or family traditions vary by household.
culture.language: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 is a common New Year greeting.

culture.title: 전화 etiquette
culture.summary: Telephone Korean uses conventional expressions such as 여보세요 and polite requests for asking to speak to someone. The exact level of politeness changes with relationship and setting.
culture.language: 여보세요 → 누구세요? → ___ 씨 좀 바꿔 주세요 → 안녕히 계세요 / 끊을게요.
